Succinctly put, the case of the prosecution is that on 03.05.2010 one Priyanka was riding pillion on scooter Bajaj Chetak bearing registration number DDO~3193 driven by her father Prabhu Dayal.

After hitting the divider, the RTV come on their side of the road and hit their scooter.
The RTV was being driven at a very high speed and in negligent manner.
Due to impact both Priyanka and her father fell down on the road.
Prabhu Dayal sustained head injury and blood started oozing out.
The RTV bus stopped after impact and the RTV driver was apprehended by the crowd which gathered at the spot.

8. The appellant has been convicted for offence punishable u/s 279/304A IPC.

It is apposite to reproduce in verbatim Section 279 and 304A IPC which read as under:-
279. Rash driving or riding on a public way.-Whoever drives any vehicle, or rides, on any public way in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.

304A. Causing death by negligence.-Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with im- prisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
Rash or negligent act is the common ingredient of both these pro- visions of law.
The element of rashness or negligence is a sine- qua-non for offence punishable u/s 279/304A IPC.
The burden to prove the element of rashness or negligence is on the prosecu- tion.
Ordinarily the principle of res ipsa loquitur can not be re- sorted to, in order to prove element of rashness or negligence.

While discussing section 279 and 304A IPC the High Court of Delhi in the case of Abdul Subhan vs State (Nct Of Delhi), (2006) 133 DLT 562; observed as follows:-

sentences.text: As observed in Badri Prasad (supra), to establish the offence either under Section 279 or Section 304A, the commission of a rash and negligent act has to be proved.

The only distinction being that in Section 279, rash and negligent act relates to the manner of driving or riding on a public way while the offence under Section 304A extends to any rash and negligent act falling short of culpable homicide.
As correctly observed by the learned judge, the rashness or negligence which needs to be established is something more than a mere error of judgment.

There is also a distinction between rashness and negligence in that, rashness conveys the idea of doing a reckless act without considering any of its consequences whereas negligence connotes want of proper care.

'Rash Driving' refers to driving with a reckless disregard for safety, often knowing the potential for causing harm whereas 'Negligent Driving' involves a failure to exercise reasonable care leading to unintended consequences.
Rash or negligent driving has to be examined in the light of facts and circumstances of a given case (See Ravi Kapur vs. State of Rajasthan, (2012) 9 SCC 284).

PW4 Priyanka had stated that RTV came at very high speed from the opposite side and after breaking the divider hit against their scooter.
During her cross-examination, at one point she stated that she could not tell the exact or approximate speed as she did not drive any vehicle though the speed was less.

sentences.text: PW2, PW4, PW8 and PW10 SI Suresh Sharma had con- firmed the presence of divider on the road where the accident oc- curred.
PW2 and PW4 had also deposed that the RTV was on the opposite side of the road.
In fact, PW4 Priyanka had categori- cally stated that the RTV crossed over the divider and hit their scooter.
The mechanical inspection report of RTV (Ex.PW12/B) shows that only its front bumper was damaged but it was road- worthy.
The mechanical inspection report of scooter (Ex.PW12/A) shows that it had sustained considerable damage on the front, left as well as right side and it was rendered unfit for driving.
From the damage sustained by both vehicles, it can be safely deduced that both the vehicles had a head on collision due to which the scooter got unbalanced and hit against the road.
It is noteworthy that the RTV even after the accident was fit for being plyed on road.
Hence, even the possibility of mechanical failure resulting in the RTV crossing over the divider to other side of the road is negated.
The only possible conclusion that can be drawn is that the driver lost control over the RTV and caused accident on the other side of road.

With respect, in our opinion, both the grounds are invalid.

For, in the circumstances of the case, she was the only and most natural witness; she was the only person present in the hut with the deceased at the time of the occurrence, and the only person who saw the occurrence.

True, it is she is the wife Abdul Jabbar vs State Of Delhi on 7 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/91145563/

sentences.text: She is related to the deceased.
'Related' is not equivalent to 'interested'.
A witness may be called 'interested' only when he or she derives some benefit from the result of a litigation; in the decree in a civil case, or in seeing an accused person punished.
A witness who is a natural one and is the only possible eye witness in the circumstances of a case cannot be said to be 'interested'.
In the instant case P.W.1 had no interest in protecting the real culprit, and falsely implicating the respondents.
PW4 Priyanka has nothing to gain by falsely implicating accused in the present case.
Her presence at the time and place of accident is natural and does not arouse suspicion.
It is not uncommon for a daughter to ride pillion on her father's scooter.
PW2 had also confirmed that a female was riding pillion on the scooter which met with an accident on 03.05.2010 at Jheel Chowk.
Moreover, the accident occurred at about 1:30 PM and Rukka in the case was prepared at 3:30 PM on the basis of statement of Priyanka.

The manner in which the testimony of an eye witness is to be appreciated, has been laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Balu Sudam Khalde vs The State of Maharashtra 2023 SCC Online SC 355; as under:-

sentences.text: The appreciation of ocular evidence is a hard task.
There is no fixed or straight-jacket formula for appreciation of the ocular evidence.

The judicially evolved principles for appreciation of ocular evidence in a criminal case can be enumerated as under:
"I.
While appreciating the evidence of a witness, the approach must be whether the evidence of the witness read as a whole appears to have a ring of truth.

Once that impression is formed, it is undoubtedly necessary for the Court to scrutinize the evidence more particularly keeping in view the deficiencies, drawbacks and infirmities pointed out in the evidence as a whole and evaluate them to find out whether it is against the general tenor of the evidence given by the witness and whether the earlier evaluation of the evidence is shaken as to render it unworthy of belief.

II. If the Court before whom the witness gives evidence had the opportunity to form the opinion about the general tenor of evidence given by the witness, the appellate court which had not this benefit will have to attach due weight to the appreciation of evidence by the trial court and unless there are reasons weighty and formidable it would not be proper to reject the evidence on the ground of minor variations or Crl.

sentences.text: III. When eye-witness is examined at length it is quite possible for him to make some discrepancies.

But courts should bear in mind that it is only when discrepancies in the evidence of a witness are so incompatible with the credibility of his version that the court is justified in jettisoning his evidence.
IV.

Minor discrepancies on trivial matters not touching the core of the case, hyper technical approach by taking sentences torn out of context here or there from the evidence, attaching importance to some technical error committed by the investigating officer not going to the root of the matter would not ordinarily permit rejection of the evidence as a whole.

V. Too serious a view to be adopted on mere variations falling in the narration of an incident (either as between the evidence of two witnesses or as between two statements of the same witness) is an unrealistic approach for judicial scrutiny.
VI. By and large a witness cannot be expected to possess a photographic memory and to recall the details of an incident.
It is not as if a video tape is replayed on the mental screen.
VII. Ordinarily it so happens that a witness is overtaken by events.
The witness could not have anticipated the occurrence which so often has an element of surprise.
The mental faculties therefore cannot be expected to be attuned to absorb the details.
VIII. The powers of observation differ from person to person.

What one may notice,
another may not.
An object or movement might emboss its image on one person's mind whereas it might go unnoticed on the part of another.
IX. By and large people cannot accurately recall a conversation and reproduce the very words used by them or heard by them.
They can only recall the main purport of the conversation.
It is unrealistic to expect a witness to be a human tape recorder.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The burden to prove the element of rashness or negligence is on the prosecu- tion.
Ordinarily the principle of res ipsa loquitur can not be re- sorted to, in order to prove element of rashness or negligence.
The only distinction being that in Section 279, rash and negligent act relates to the manner of driving or riding on a public way while the offence under Section 304A extends to any rash and negligent act falling short of culpable homicide.
As correctly observed by the learned judge, the rashness or negligence which needs to be established is something more than a mere error of judgment.
There is also a distinction between rashness and negligence in that, rashness conveys the idea of doing a reckless act without considering any of its consequences whereas negligence connotes want of proper care.
'Rash Driving' refers to driving with a reckless disregard for safety, often knowing the potential for causing harm whereas 'Negligent Driving' involves a failure to exercise reasonable care leading to unintended consequences.
Rash or negligent driving has to be examined in the light of facts and circumstances of a given case (See Ravi Kapur vs. State of Rajasthan, (2012) 9 SCC 284).
In the case at hand, the prosecution has to prove that Abdul Jabbar was driving the RTV bus in a rash or negligent manner and while driving the RTV in such manner, he caused the acci- dent wherein Prabhu Dayal lost his life.
The prosecution has not been able to place on record any credible evidence to show the speed at which the RTV was being driven at the time of acci- dent.
Merely stating that a vehicle was at high speed does not ipso facto lead to an inference that the same was being driven in a rash or negligent manner.
